subtype: Approach: nagging and repeating the demand [Pitfall]
passage: Every afternoon Mina met her mother, Astrid, at the door with the same words: "Can I have a phone now? Everyone has one." On Monday Astrid said not yet. On Tuesday Mina asked again, louder. On Wednesday she cried on the stairs, and Astrid stayed quiet and firm. On Thursday Mina stamped her foot, and her father said, "Enough. The answer will not change if you ask ten times." By Friday Mina had stopped saying anything at all, and dinner was tense. Astrid's face looked tired more than angry. Mina had never once said why she needed a phone or what she would do to use it carefully.

qa.q: On which day did Mina cry on the stairs?
qa.a: Mina cried on the stairs on Wednesday.

qa.q: What might Mina be feeling as she stamped her foot on Thursday?
qa.a: Frustrated and disappointed, because each refusal made her angrier and asking again was not working.

qa.q: What different approach might have earned Mina a better hearing, and why?
qa.a: She could ask once, calmly at a good moment, with reasons and a plan for using it carefully, because parents can weigh reasons but pressure only makes them firmer.

qa.q: How does Mina's asking look to Astrid by the end of the week?
qa.a: Wearing: Astrid looks tired rather than angry, and every repeat gives her more reason to stay firm.

grounding: A child asks for a phone daily and cries when refused, and the parents grow firmer because pressure gives them no reasons.

subtype: Approach: nagging and repeating the demand [Pitfall]
passage: At the parent-teacher meeting, Wasim's mother had just sat down in front of Mrs Menon when Wasim started again. "Everyone in my class has a phone. Please, Ammi, please." It was the eleventh day in a row. He had asked at breakfast, in the auto, at dinner, and now here, in the classroom, with other parents waiting. When his mother shook her head, his eyes filled and his voice got loud. Mrs Menon looked up. Wasim's mother said quietly, "We never said never. But every time he cries, it's harder to even think about it." On the way out she told him, "No phone talk for a month." Wasim kicked the gate. Before the meeting, the answer had been "not yet". Now it was a month of nothing.

qa.q: How many days in a row had Wasim asked?
What was Wasim feeling when his eyes filled?
qa.a: Frustrated and upset, desperate for a yes.

qa.q: What other approach might have worked better for Wasim?
qa.a: Asking once, calmly, with his reasons and how he would use a phone, and accepting 'not yet' as a real answer.

qa.q: How does Wasim's mother experience the pressure?
qa.a: She finds the crying makes it harder even to think about a phone, so she becomes firmer.

grounding: A child who nags and cries for a phone every day makes his mother firmer, turning 'not yet' into a month of no.

subtype: Approach: nagging and repeating the demand [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Charu, Madhav's older sister. For two weeks Madhav has asked Papa for a phone every single day. First at breakfast. Then when Papa came home, before he'd even taken his shoes off. Then through the bathroom door. When Papa said no, Madhav cried loudly, and once threw his school bag. He never said what he needed the phone for, only "I want it" and "You never give me anything." At first Papa said, "Maybe for your birthday." Last night Papa said, "Now the answer is no until next year." Madhav looked shocked. I think he really believed that asking more would work. I don't know what he's feeling today; he hasn't said a word about phones at all.

qa.q: How long has Madhav been asking for a phone?
What might Madhav be feeling after Papa's new answer?
qa.a: Shocked, and perhaps regretful that asking more made things worse.

qa.q: What else could Madhav have tried?
qa.a: Explaining what he needs a phone for and agreeing to wait for his birthday with some rules.

qa.q: How does Charu see what happened?
qa.a: Charu thinks Madhav believed nagging would work, and notices his silence about phones today.

grounding: A sister watches a child's daily nagging and crying for a phone turn a 'maybe' into a firm no.
